concepts.statement: What makes a delivery model cloud computing: computing services as a whole — not one service class such as storage or websites — delivered over the internet, on demand, from capacity someone else operates
Which party owns which layer of the stack under the shared responsibility model, and how the split moves as the service type shifts from on-premises through IaaS and PaaS to SaaS
Telling public, private and hybrid cloud apart by where the infrastructure sits, who operates it and who else shares it — ownership and tenancy, not geography, decide the model
Reading a described situation — its capital constraints, control demands, compliance posture and existing estate — and picking the cloud deployment model those constraints force
vocabulary: appropriate use cases for each cloud model

concepts.statement: Paying for what is actually used rather than what is provisioned: the consumption-based model means no upfront purchase, cost that stops when use stops, and a bill that tracks demand

Classifying spend when infrastructure moves to the cloud: owned datacenter assets are capital expenditure, rented cloud services are operational expenditure, and a migration converts one profile into the other
Choosing between pay-as-you-go flexibility and a term commitment: a steady, long-lived workload is the case for committed capacity at a discount, and flexibility is what the discount costs
Recognising when interruptible spare capacity is the right buy: the lowest compute price, paid for with eviction risk, fits workloads that tolerate being stopped and resumed
What serverless removes from the customer's responsibility — no instances to provision, scale or pay for while idle — and what it does not remove: the code, its configuration and its data
Staying available through component failure: high availability as a designed property, expressed as an uptime expectation and achieved through redundancy rather than through better single components
Growing capacity on the right axis: vertical scaling resizes the existing resource, horizontal scaling adds or removes instances — and a described change in demand points at exactly one of the two
Separating two benefits that sound alike: reliability is recovering from failure and continuing to function; predictability is knowing in advance what performance and cost will be

What the platform contributes to security and governance as a benefit of adopting cloud: policy control, patch currency and network protections supplied by the platform that a customer would otherwise build and staff

Manageability as a benefit: administering the estate through the platform's own tooling and automation — scaling, monitoring and deployment handled by the platform, reachable from anywhere — rather than by hand

What the customer still owns when the provider supplies virtualised infrastructure: the operating system and everything above it — patching, runtime, middleware, data — with maximum control as the price of maximum responsibility

What the provider absorbs when it supplies the platform: the operating system, runtime and middleware leave the customer's plate while the application and its data remain — the middle position on the responsibility ladder
What is left to configure when the provider supplies the finished application: features and users, nothing beneath them — least responsibility and least control, licensed rather than built

Reading a workload's control requirements, team and time-to-value against the three service types and picking the one the constraints force — needing OS patching control forces IaaS, wanting no operations at all points at SaaS
vocabulary: appropriate use cases for each cloud service type (IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS)

concepts.statement: What an Azure region is — a latency-bounded set of datacenters, not a single facility and not a zone — and why many regions are paired with a distant partner region for platform-level replication and sequenced updates
Sovereign regions as nationally isolated Azure instances built for government and residency obligations — a separate cloud with its own boundary, not a deployment model and not just another region

Availability zones as physically separated facilities inside one region with independent power, cooling and networking — the construct that survives the loss of an entire datacenter, which no in-datacenter construct does

What a resource group bounds and what it does not: a resource belongs to exactly one group at a time, group-level settings reach current and future members, and membership does not constrain where members may be located
The subscription as the billing and access boundary that owns resource groups — and its relationship to identity: many subscriptions can trust the same directory tenant

The containment chain read in order — resource, resource group, subscription, management group — what each level exists to bound, why governance at scale is applied at the level above subscriptions, and what inherits down the chain
vocabulary: hierarchy of resource groups, subscriptions, and management groups

concepts.statement: Choosing among virtual machines, containers and functions by what the workload needs you to manage: a whole operating system, a packaged runtime, or nothing but event-driven code that runs on demand

The virtual-machine family constructs and what each buys: scale sets run identical managed instances that grow and shrink with demand, availability sets stagger update and fault domains inside a datacenter, and Azure Virtual Desktop delivers the desktop itself as a service

What a virtual machine cannot exist without: the dependent resources — disk, network interface, virtual network membership, and a public address only if it must be reachable — created alongside it and billed as themselves
vocabulary: the resources required for virtual machines

concepts.statement: Choosing where an application runs when several hosts could technically serve it: the managed web-app host against containers against raw virtual machines, decided by how much of the host the team wants to own

Virtual-network semantics: a virtual network is isolated by default, subnets segment it internally and route to one another by default, and Azure DNS manages name resolution with the same credentials and tooling as the rest of the estate

Choosing the connectivity construct by who is connecting and what constraint dominates: an encrypted tunnel over the internet — site-to-site for a network, point-to-site for a single client — a private circuit when latency and predictability rule, and peering for VNet-to-VNet over the backbone

Reaching a service across the public internet versus privately from inside a virtual network over the Microsoft backbone — what a public endpoint exposes and what a private endpoint removes from the attack surface

Matching the storage service and type to the data's shape and access pattern: blobs for unstructured objects at scale, files for SMB shares on a UNC path, disks for VM volumes, queues for small transient messages, tables for schemaless key-attribute data

Trading storage price against access price over a data lifetime: the frequent-access tier costs most to hold and least to read, the archive tier the reverse — the right rung is read off the access pattern, not the data's importance
Reading the redundancy ladder by copies, distance and the failure class each rung survives — and choosing down as well as up: the cheapest option is the correct one when the data is expendable

Choosing the file-movement tool by direction, volume and repeat-frequency: scripted bulk copy from the command line, a graphical browse-and-transfer client, or continuous two-way sync that keeps an on-premises share and Azure Files in step
Choosing a migration path by data volume against network feasibility: the assessment-and-migration service when the wire can carry the data in the time available, shipped appliances when it cannot

The cloud directory as the identity authority for users, applications and devices — one tenant serving cloud and synchronised on-premises identities alike — and the separate managed-domain service for workloads that still need legacy domain protocols

Proving who someone is versus deciding what they may do — and the named capabilities on the proving side: one sign-in across many applications, a second factor such as a one-time code or token, and removing the password entirely
Letting partners and customers who are not in your tenant collaborate without creating accounts in it — external identities as the construct for boundary-crossing access

Deciding at sign-in time, from signals such as location, device state and detected risk, what a user must satisfy before access is granted — policy evaluated at the point of authentication, not a standing permission

Role-based access control read both ways: what a single role assignment bounds — its actions, at its scope, inherited downward — and how multiple assignments combine: as the union of what they grant, never the intersection

Telling the two security models apart by what each prescribes: Zero Trust assumes the network is already hostile and verifies every request explicitly; the defense-in-depth model layers controls so one breached layer is not a breached system

Continuous security-posture assessment and threat protection across the estate — including the regulatory-compliance view of the infrastructure — as distinct from governing and classifying the data that lives in it
What bills and when for resources that already exist: a stopped virtual machine still pays for its storage, a resource group itself is free, and every resource meters separately on its own terms
vocabulary: factors that can affect costs in Azure

concepts.statement: The cost levers fixed at design time — resource type and size, region choice, network egress, and licensing options — and which of them a described bill difference points at
vocabulary: factors that can affect costs in Azure

concepts.statement: Estimating what a design that does not exist yet would cost — the pricing calculator's job, and precisely the thing a spend-analysis tool cannot do
Analysing spend that has already happened — slicing incurred cost by resource, service and time to find what is driving it — as the retrospective half of cost management
Guarding spend before it overruns: budgets set the line and alerts fire as consumption approaches it — the proactive half of cost management, as distinct from analysing what was already spent

Attaching metadata to resources so cost and ownership can be sliced after the fact: tags cut across the containment hierarchy rather than replacing it, and carry the department or application dimension chargeback needs
Governing and classifying the data estate — discovering, mapping and protecting sensitive information wherever it travels — rather than governing the resource estate the data happens to sit on

Azure Policy as the deployment-time gate: define what compliant looks like once and non-compliant resources are prevented from being created anywhere in scope — restricting allowed regions is the canonical case
Azure Policy over the estate that already exists: evaluating current resources against standards, surfacing the non-compliant ones, and applying enforcement to new and existing deployments alike
A resource lock blocks deletion or modification independently of who holds permissions — it stops an owner too, and must be deliberately removed before the guarded action can proceed

Placing the right control class against the obligation: policy gates what may be created, a lock protects what exists regardless of permission, and role assignments decide who may attempt either — and only one of the three stops an owner deleting
The graphical control plane: right for exploration, visualisation and one-off administration — and wrong for anything that must be repeatable, reviewable or performed at scale

The three command surfaces told apart: a browser-hosted, pre-authenticated shell that needs no local install, and two command languages it can run — the cross-platform CLI and the object-based PowerShell
Extending Azure's management plane to what does not run in Azure: on-premises and other-cloud resources projected into Azure and governed with the same tooling as native ones
Declaring the desired estate as a versioned artefact rather than clicking it into existence — what infrastructure as code buys: repeatability, review before deployment, and drift you can see

Azure Resource Manager as the control plane every deployment and management request goes through, whatever surface issued it — and its declarative template format that makes repeat deployments identical

Personalised best-practice recommendations across cost, security, reliability, performance and operational excellence — produced by analysing resources that already exist, which is what separates the recommender from an estimator or an enforcer

Three different questions about the same outage: is the platform having an incident at all, is it affecting my services and regions, and is this specific resource healthy — each answered by a different health surface

Azure Monitor as the telemetry platform for the whole estate — collecting, correlating and acting on metrics and logs from many resources in one place; the named surfaces are parts of the platform, not rivals to it
Log Analytics as the query surface: the place collected log data is interrogated and analysed — where you ask questions of telemetry, not the pipeline that gathers it and not the layer that notifies

Azure Monitor alerts as the notification-and-action layer: watching a signal for a condition and firing when it is met — telling you and triggering a response, as distinct from storing or querying telemetry

Application-level telemetry: performance anomalies, request failures and usage inside the application itself — the application surface of the telemetry platform, distinct from the platform-level collection beneath it
